Dr. Knubble & His Bellyfloss
A Novel by
Chuck Tingle
It starts with my first ever encounter with love, I mean actual human romantic love between women. I was eight at the time, and my father took me on a trip out west with his family to meet my grandmother who had come all the way from Canada. This meeting, the granddaddy-busting reunion that it proved to be, would prove a defining moment not just in my childhood life, but for many other people too, and it all came down to my cousin Milly and her best friend Amy—I
. . . now it is your turn, Mr. Pynchon!

Okay fine whatever, we get it: Miley and Amy. But please don't call them that, I'm still angry about it (even if Miley did say she wasn't really pissed off anymore). In any case, it was these two friends of mine, plus their mother Gretta—who'd brought over some maple syrup she made herself from her sugar tree out in the yard back home in Quebec province—who decided to throw a party to show my father and me our great auntie Nana's beautiful face after having passed us around so much over the years without even knowing who we were, but now

suddenly here we were standing right in front of her smiling, talking to us, hugging and touching. So what could've possibly happened after that, Mr. T? Well like I said earlier, it was my father and me that found ourselves falling deeply head over heels for one of those beautiful creatures from across the sea—but then the whole thing changed for me. It changed because Milly and Gretta began showing an almost maternal interest in me—they gave me presents; things they thought might catch the eye and interest me—and their affection for me turned into genuine caring for me in a way that neither my father

or I have known since—so maybe the most surprising aspect of this tale is how the rest of our journey back home was actually quite peaceful as far as my emotions went, until the very end, when something horrible, unspeakably horrible indeed occurred. Something, I believe, that changed me irrevocably forever and led me onto the road to self discovery which would eventually take me all the way to this book—that of course, being this book—and that is the story you will hear below. Or at least, you would, had the publisher allowed us to write this chapter in the style of the great H

. Pym, and included footnotes throughout, instead of letting you experience this entire journey through our writing the story as we see fit. Oh sure the author can explain everything and tell you where you're going wrong and why, but really there's nothing more frustrating and infuriating than to have someone else tell you the obvious and then fail to acknowledge their own faults—which, if anything, only makes the person who has the fault feel more stupid and foolish for their error, whereas when you yourself are told, oh you know you got it completely backward, the knowledge helps make you look less silly, and thus you begin

:
Chapter 1:

Dr. Knubble And The Bellyflops
I never realized before just how funny and weird it must've been, the way you could be sitting in a car driving down a highway at a high rate of speed and then stop for a second, maybe go twenty feet and do another three or four seconds of accelerating and stop again, then do another ten or fifteen seconds of acceleration and finally pull over to park the car, the person getting into the driver’s seat looking straight ahead at the passing scenery with a sort of intense expression, their arms hanging out of the open window, and the person in the

passenger seat who’d been sitting next to them just watching out the window while saying, I wonder how fast this vehicle would be going if we kept driving it at this pace?
I had this same sort of expression on my face the first time, only that’s exactly the moment I met Dr. Robert A. "Bob" Knubble.
Dr. Knubble and Miley Cyrus
A novel by:
Thomas Pynchon & Chuck Tingle
This all took place a couple weeks later, and my first impression was this.

Wow I think to myself, the only reason we even bothered to stop here is so I could see a man in an orange suit. But then he looks at me in that calm and relaxed fashion he has, the smile coming over him and his whole body shaking slightly, causing a soft vibration that’s not too hard and yet not quite enough to send a thrill up and down your spinal column either—he smiles like he knows something special is about to happen, and I am so struck by the feeling, which seems both sweet and powerful at the same time, that the sight and his manner, plus the smell of

that fresh-sanded woodsy aroma I always find so relaxing and uplifting, causes me somehow to surrender to this overwhelming emotion of a deep desire to just relax and be with him—it feels as if the universe has given us permission, and I don't even want to know why—this was the exact moment when I decided that my whole purpose in life now consisted not of trying to become a great artist, nor of becoming famous and respected for having created something important—instead I now wished only for an ordinary life where the most beautiful and precious things would appear to be what they actually were, that is: totally

unexpected events—in short, all the good stuff that can happen between two strangers on a road trip with a mother who brought them maple syrup.
I was thinking about this whole situation as I walked around inside Dr. Knubble's office and checked the appointment books—all filled to capacity, with many new patients in for consultations already waiting their turn—while the old doctor was in one of the back rooms examining and giving advice and guidance to some lucky and wealthy client. I didn't really understand all the terms being used and heard the words 'brevoxen', 'bifidophorus', and even

a little bit of 'cretacean', but that just meant 'like the crabs', so in essence what this all came down to, in the simplest of simple terms—the only terms the people around me needed to grasp at that moment—was I knew for certain now, after my own recent personal transformation into something more and better than before, I now felt more than ready to join Dr. Knubble in helping him give other poor souls the very special chance of finding their own bliss. That’s why it was me and my mother—and the maple syrup that Gretta carried around with her

like a purse or pocketbook or whatever you call it that we brought back from Canada with her—who decided it was best for me to accompany her on our way back east when the three-day family vacation was over, and I remember my mother asking if she could stay a week in New Jersey or Pennsylvania somewhere so she wouldn't have any excuses if Milly got pregnant while we still lived there—as I recall, this idea was shot down by Amy immediately, saying she'd never be able to forgive Milly or herself.

Then Milly, being who she was and always trying to keep a handle of control over all the situations and people and things in the world and the cosmos and the planet and everything that happens in it and on it, said if you and your sister can get along without you, I certainly won’t be holding my breath and waiting until the baby is born before the whole damn thing starts going off and exploding again.

And that of course set us up for our roadtrip, though I wasn't to learn of this right away, because the truth about why I ended up in that particular location on the road—and it would have seemed completely random if it weren't for all those years my father spent studying and learning how everything worked and how it all fit together; he taught me a lot—is I guess you could call it the ultimate accident, but really just part of the natural order of the universe.

Okay well first off, the car my father drove was the old green Honda Civic. He and my mom always had that car in perfect condition, no matter what kind of terrible mess it looked and sounded in, and whenever we needed money to go anywhere or do anything or take a break and go to the mall or something to eat, it just miraculously appeared out of thin air, usually within twenty-four hours—not even thirty-six! My mother, bless her soul, believed the world was run and ordered by forces far greater than any individual person, so when I once asked her how she did something so
--here Pynchon falls asleep, and Chuck Tingle takes over the narrative for the duration of Pynchon's sleepytime:

I believe in a great big world where everyone gets along. Like we always talk about in school and everybody wants everybody else’s business to succeed, and all that. Well I believe that sometimes the whole plan goes out the window, even with my dad driving the car like I am, which is why I feel we should make a quick exit and start heading north to a nearby motel, but I know we must stick to our current route or the universe might send someone who can tell what’s happened, so I ask myself how could that happen?

And the answer comes as if it is written on a blackboard: We would have made a sudden turn into that parking space—there, by the bank—to stop to use one of their bathrooms and maybe buy a magazine—I forget which magazine—that would be where the whole problem occurred.
So then we come upon that empty space that was just waiting to receive my dear friend Chuck, and when I pull up to the spot next—” ‘To be continued’ the voice behind my left shoulder whispers into the ear that is always closest to him—the moment my eyes are open and the door

shuts itself and the seat moves down to reveal the sweetest most wonderful ass I've ever laid eyes on in all of human existence—which of course I'm only too happy to discover—a man walks up, he says hi to both me and my father in that very friendly manner people often adopt when trying not to appear suspicious and creepy. But since I'm a pretty smart guy I can easily pick up on his feelings about all this and it becomes obvious what is really bothering him: This is a place for married people and families, so how dare a guy like me be coming in there and sitting with them, as

if there wasn't some rule against doing that? It's almost comical how I immediately become embarrassed, and I don't know what the rules say in terms of being able to park right here without anyone getting mad, or being charged for this spot, but anyway it feels like a whole lot more is at stake here, and it is only when my dad looks around the car and asks if we shouldn't drive off right now before things go from bad to worse—because this isn't exactly what you’d call normal, right?

That's why the two men get all tense. I mean my mother has gone back to sleep after having the dream again and my father and I, the poor sap that just had a dream that is now making me even less inclined to want to be near him anymore, have no idea that there are actually people living in that building across from us, with families, with lives of their own. So I try really hard to remain calm while telling myself that this could be any ordinary motel, but instead of saying that I also think the world might actually come crashing down and destroy itself in a fiery blaze if that happens—which

is the only real reason why it doesn't—instead, I say:
“What? Did I hear my name called out there? I’m sorry. You just said, did I hear your name called out there? Yes you certainly heard my friend calling me Chuckie over here, but you need to watch out for that—some folks who work at a lot of motels around the area and other places like this will try very hard to pretend they didn't notice a young couple walking up and sitting right down there

beside them and all that stuff. I guess you should have been paying closer attention to who you’re talking with and whether or not there's someone who works at the motel sitting over there listening in to every word, so of course he can’t help but notice when my mom wakes up screaming—that would definitely make sense if she had done it a hundred times in front of people—and that makes my daddy realize that we really ought to be heading off somewhere before someone calls an ambulance for the rest of you.
Both Tingle and Pynchon are awake and dawdling over chapter 2. You can see their literary scuffles in (parenthesis):

“And the whole thing about why he decided to call himself 'Thomas P. Sample,' which I think it's a little weird and strange to start off the book that way, you have to know how much time and effort it took my old man to research that kind of crap. All kinds of things had happened in the history of this town, which meant it made him a big believer and advocate of researching anything and everything, no matter how seemingly useless and stupid it seemed, so naturally when we got out there it wasn't too difficult to find somebody who'd worked at the place before and who was still living
Chapter 2: There Lies the Knubbins

!
 A small child runs up the sidewalk. The child looks like it belongs in the circus. I wonder if I can run up the same way—I try it—my foot catches on the uneven sidewalk. I slip on the loose asphalt and slide backwards, bumping my head painfully. Then another one pops up. This kid is running towards the parking lot and is wearing shorts so long I have to keep a constant lookout for them, which causes the whole time-lag problem that I’ve mentioned, but this time it doesn’t matter because by the time I catch sight of the kid

my friend Chuck Tingle’s already got him! He's got his hands wrapped tightly in a large towel that he holds in front of him. Tingle stops short.
The two children are running together and yelling excitedly, and it sounds like “Mommy”. They both jump over a hedge, but the older boy loses his balance and lands in a crouched position with a heavy splash, but Tingle catches the younger child before he gets up. I run to them and look over the little guy’s head to see his mother, a thin woman who is holding her hands to

her cheeks as if in shock and staring up with big wide eyes into Tingle’s face. She is dressed very formally—black shoes, gray slacks and a white silk shirt—and I notice for the first time that her hair has begun to gray. As I approach her I notice a slight smell in the air. The scent of decay seems stronger today, like it might even have some faint hint of sulfur or hydrogen sulfide about it...I know I’ve never noticed this before and maybe that means the situation is only getting stranger and scarier?
(Let us make this Black Mirror scary. Existential sci fi dread, whaddya say Pynch?)

Anyway as the mother and I approach she begins talking in a slow monotone, the voice almost dead: “We just moved in, and we don’t know any neighbors—it’s all brand new construction, no one’s around—we haven’t met anyone yet, and this isn’t a good place for kids. This neighborhood isn’t good for kids at all. What is that man doing? We’re in our bathtub—I don’t want the water to go all dirty and stinky, you know what a tub is
(how about a lab where all viruses are birthed from a scientific penis.)

I can’t let the little guy run out into traffic, there might be an accident. This is a bad, unsafe place for children. I just wanted a fresh start in a nice new place and everything, I’m sorry if we disturbed you but this area is too dangerous for my son. He should be home with me—he’s only three and a half, I’ll give you my number, I’m sorry we intruded. I don’t want to bother you anymore.
(But the scientific penis knows no bounds, eh Pynchie?)

You shouldn’t have brought that towel—that thing is bad for him, the germs—no germs, he won’t have to get sick—I hope, I hope—this neighborhood has too many homeless and crazy old ladies and junkies and that is the last place we should be. Please take care, bye. And my apologies, you are free to do with him whatever you want, we can pay—but please call the cops, we were scared—”
Tingle looks at the mother and then takes a long look at the child and then says:
"You
are now in a Pynchon/Tingle joint. We have written you in! Do you have any requests before you take on a life of your own?

Chapter 4, The Biggest Thing of All
The following day—a Monday—after having a nightmare for which my brain is now very tired of remembering the details, it was only because I didn’t want to sleep that I found the strength and determination to wake up, get dressed and come down the hall to check things out, which in the dream had been my father and me walking around this house in some kind of secret location.
Now in real life there are people living here in various places all the time—people with their lives going forward, who would like to be left alone, or at
least unbothered by hootenany.

And I can see where they would need privacy, even if only a temporary reprieve. So what if we don’t know where these other tenants of ours have gone for good. It may not even mean anything that there’s someone living over our heads who is so intent on keeping to himself. But the dream I’d had last night was much too intense and involved to leave things like it—it seemed as if my mind were still looking back into a very different time and space, and in order to understand why it felt so necessary to investigate, I thought I needed some clues about the world
(cue the membrane between the worlds!)

that I was coming out of. Maybe I should find a friend who could read this story and tell me exactly what is meant by it all, a way for us both to better get through it, as the saying goes: the truth, my friend, shall set you right? Or even better than a friend who could interpret: a stranger, maybe someone whose mind has become totally and forever disconnected from the reality we all live in. A completely alien being, an outsider of some sort who would see what I’m trying to show, and then tell me how it’s really meant.

In other words, a psychic or an intuitive! That’s always been the easiest explanation for why so few of us actually ever seem to hear voices, but now that it has been explained for me—in more ways and in more depth than I ever wanted to know about—what are the alternatives, and is it even worth thinking about? Is it worth investigating further and asking about what happened after I’ve gone through the door, if I don’t believe I’ll go inside, because in the future, the real future, I can imagine that the door will open into an even more
orthoganal set of alternate futures. Ones that are not too drastically diffetent than this one.

I guess maybe there won’t be much of a future after I get to it—maybe it’s just like in the dreams where the characters die at the beginning of the movie? What does that say about me?
I am getting confused and I am also starting to worry about whether or not it might help me in the end, or even before that—if I keep putting these two strange ideas together and letting them get all tangled and twisted and confusing.
(Is this too meta? Tingle asks Pynchon, who just stares at him for an answer.)

So as a matter of self-preservation it would be best to put all this aside, and move along. I think it might make me feel a little less weird about this whole situation, if the person living above me were to take action to stop it all from happening—I don’t want to have any more nightmares, but maybe it’s just something in the air here?
It was at breakfast, where Maxine sat beside her husband and talked with his face, when she first saw it.

I can’t say she saw the exact moment that he started, or realized, because she didn’t know for certain if this had already begun, but the look on his face had to indicate that there might be a change. And the smell! If there was an odiferous element, she had yet to figure it out—it wasn’t the typical musky male funk that we’re all familiar with, but there certainly was a whiff in the atmosphere that couldn’t quite be pinned down.
Pheromones of alarm, and a beacon to similar others. It was later found out, after the final scrapings were done on the battlefield.

That some women who’d lost their partners, even those who still hadn’t had children, did have a tendency to start searching for men—and sometimes find one of a type that seemed like they might fit better, a little too well perhaps—and then there were a few cases in the literature where the opposite happened.
There were three things I learned in college about the female reproductive system, which helped in coming up with some of the explanations for these events that I witnessed during that terrible summer, although my knowledge and understanding of biology came only as a very rough sketch of a few facts that could apply

.
Firstly, and most basic: The ovaries contain eggs. The spermatozoa are contained by testes and produce an enzyme, which has the power to convert the egg. When this process takes place it causes fertilization of that egg. Once this happens the body becomes involved, as a woman can carry the child in some form until the umbilical cord comes off and the infant starts living outside its mother. There are no longer any organs inside the uterus, other than some muscle cells. It’s only in our heads and hearts and lungs that it seems we remain connected, at least at a

.
Second, the eggs are sadly not edible. Af juju

Even with a very fine scalpel, a skilled hand or the latest equipment—none of these can create an ova without damage to it or its contents. This has made us realize how incredibly complex the biological structure really is.
Thirdly, the vagina is the only part inside the female that a man may access, as long as the walls are open. And while the walls of some are more pliable than others, it still must be a woman’s sole right to control the flow of blood in this area.
Fourthly, woman are waiting for the one true menstruater that can control the bloodflows over all women across tume

, the entire globe!
I was able to come to this fourth discovery through observation of all the females around us who had just experienced it for the very first time, the very last ones I’d expected. The very few who were still young and innocent enough to experience it once again and not be afraid of anything.
As a matter of curiosity I went into the hospital bathroom after work the day after my wife told me about the event. After having gone in the bathroom the next several times I felt a bit better and more secure in my role, like I’d gotten permission to look.

And it didn’t take me long to realize I needed some sort of guide for what I should be seeing and what I shouldn’t, as the other guys around the house who also knew the story had warned: "Watch it for the worst stuff, and stay outta sight, and try to ignore it."
And after a little while of trying hard to get it through to myself that there might not have been any real need for me to see any of the images at all (because they could’ve changed in the future, just because of me going down the street), that what it really

meant was that maybe I didn’t actually know much about it—not like I had to know the ins and outs or anything like I thought, it just wasn’t like I was getting anywhere with that particular question.
And that the thing was—if there were such people living here in town—they could easily change themselves to avoid being seen or recognized, so that wouldn’t necessarily give them away either. It’s just that it was kind of nice having somebody tell me all the rules and boundaries for now, like an older brother I never got

who would take me places where the others wouldn’t follow me—like down the alley to the dumpsters, or up the back fire escape to watch girls pee from the top.
The best way I can explain it is like it would be for me if I were in another world—in one where things happen differently, but where there are still the same things. I guess the only difference is that there aren’t any pictures in this alternate version of mine, no movies playing in the theatre, just books that are printed and bound by machine instead of being done with a quill, paper pulp,

and a printing press. But the books do look different too—more beautiful, more intricate, a little strange to me. And the people who live there don’t look like the ones in our world anymore. The men wear suits and women have hats that hide the face and make their hair seem longer—it’s almost like they can’t trust us anymore, that we might turn against them.
And there are no other bookshelves around me, not any more anyway. There are lots of empty places though—places with all sorts of different stuff, but nothing in them at all that

seems useful or necessary to life. Some are full of clothes, but not many—it’s a very old style of wearing clothes in this other place—and nobody is walking past looking like anybody in any of the stores—all the women have on big bonnets with veils, and the dresses they do wear show a lot of bare skin underneath—no skirts, no pants. And everybody’s talking to each other using this weird language—it looks very formal, but it isn’t, because they can still talk as normal when they want.
p

I’m only learning the sounds and letters that are part of this whole alphabet of noises, the sound system they all use. It feels like an extra mouthful, and it makes it hard to talk.
So the first time that my friends, the two who are living right across the road from the park, told me that they had heard me, it scared the shit out of me. They said it was the most disgusting sounding noise they’d ever made in their lives, like it came out from a long way inside my body, like it had travelled all that distance and then burped up to

let out that sound and only I could understand it, that maybe they’d made me deaf. And that it must mean they wanted me to come over and play, so I started trying to figure out how the fuck to do that, to walk, you can’t go very far on foot in these clothes and without making any noise yourself—but there were no signs of a road or any kind of track leading to any sort of path. I just stood at the end of our street staring at it until I felt sick again.

They must’ve sensed how bad this had made me feel, and they didn’t even mention it again, because they didn’t ask if they could help—just sat there watching for ages. So eventually I went to bed, figuring it would be safer that way, like a hospital room—the beds and walls and stuff had the same look and feeling. It seemed that everything in this new home had been painted and sealed a light grey, except some areas where they’d added touches of red paint here and there.
yyy
How we play during the times of alarm:

a group of people gather at the edge of our property. Sometimes they bring food and drink with them. Other days they’ll leave some things there and come by for it afterwards, as the sun gets higher. When I arrived this time the game had been called Trots—I didn’t know what it meant until later, or even what a torsos were for that matter (although one of my teachers in college told me they looked similar to breasts)—but whatever the rules were now, there was an empty bottle in my bag with my own label written on it that was for the taking, and

everybody else was sitting down around a table of cardboard pieces—I didn’t get to know about these until later—as I joined them, a little nervous and unsure, still a stranger. But they told me how it went. Everybody takes one piece of a board, and you must go and pick it up. Then whoever it was whose space you took turns putting your pieces on. And it doesn’t matter which piece you choose—they’re all the same.

I was amazed by this. So now I was sitting in front of them, holding a plastic fork that had been used to spear some fish I couldn’t remember seeing before.
One person says, "Okay." Another, "Alrighty then," and then another, who was a girl, who spoke English, says "Here we go," to nobody. "You’ve been here for quite a while already." The others laughed at that and one guy with glasses says, in a loud, high-pitched, singsong sort of voice like a kid’s: "Hey, I got
crabs, wanna see? You pay me two bucks, and I'll corral some juicy ones!"

and everybody starts to make funny, exaggerated crab noises, like the man was making it all the way up to the back end and down the backside. I don’t laugh. Nobody does. I don’t know why not, maybe it seemed stupid to do. And so I put my piece down, but I can feel them watching me now. I’m sitting next to the man in front of me and he looks up and notices I’ve just taken a step forward. His mouth drops open for the smallest of seconds and the others laugh again—this time it sounds more sincere than
a thousand somber depositions.

One woman with long hair laughs louder than the rest. She was wearing jeans. She also wore black lipstick that glistened in the sun like the skin of a fresh kill, and there were three red flowers tattooed into her face above each eye socket. She said: “Well lookit who decided to join us!” and everybody started yelling and slapping each other on the back, except the guy in the front. He didn’t say a word—he just looked confused and frightened, like a baby duck that has been separated from its mother in the first seconds of birth, but is too small

to swim. I could hear him crying behind me somewhere as they talked over him—he was crying softly and noiselessly like the wind through leaves, and they weren’t even aware of it because it was only me, his silent friend, who heard him. It felt like the other two girls were laughing a little at my discomfort.
So then they started asking me if I’d seen anybody, and where. There’s an old white lady who always wears big sunglasses. She comes in once every few weeks with a basket on her arm full of tomatoes, but we never talk much

. She likes to watch us playing. The last time she said: "I like your friends’ games—I could do it myself, but the cards are hard to hold, they make so much noise. And when I get them to do something with the hands I want they try to take my head off and suck my blood."
They all looked really happy about it. Somebody says: “Oh man! Now we’ve got someone from our world in our little community. That makes it better, like we’re all friends and not just the weird people out on their front porch.

I guess they don’t let us get any younger, huh Maxine?" and everybody laughs at this.
And when they talk about me like that they always call me "Maxine." So I say: "I’ll help out with whatever, I like your little game, it’s like I can be part of the family. I’ll tell them how things are back in our town. We’ll have a nice story, won’t we Maxine?"
(Pynchon has quality time with the wife and so leaves me to continue the story like the supportive buckaroo I am. Ready to add the great Tingle to this shenanigan of dread.)

CHUCK TINGLE SAMPLE: "You see there was this whole system of people being put together in the dark, who only came together for their mating season—you know how the moon pulls all kinds of things into it—well this time the dark thing pulled me in, and now it seems to want a bigger, badder place to set up camp.
